explanations: Honey's high sugar concentration and acidic pH stop most microorganisms growing, so a properly stored jar does not spoil.
Cave paintings at Cuevas de la Araña in Spain show people foraging for honey at least 8,000 years ago.
Honey is sweet because of its high concentrations of fructose and glucose, and is about as sweet as sucrose.
Bees store it in honeycomb, a beeswax structure made of hundreds or thousands of hexagonal cells.
Bees gather floral nectar and refine it, in the body and in the hive, until it thickens into honey.

sources.excerpt: Due to honey's high sugar concentration and acidic pH level many microorganisms cannot grow in it and, when properly stored, honey therefore does not spoil.
Several cave paintings in Cuevas de la Araña in Spain depict humans foraging for honey at least 8,000 years ago.
Honey is sweet because of its high concentrations of the monosaccharides fructose and glucose.
The honeycomb is made up of hundreds or thousands of hexagonal cells, into which the bees regurgitate honey for storage.
Bees produce honey by gathering and then refining the sugary secretions of plants (primarily floral nectar) or the secretions of other insects, like the honeydew of aphids.

editorNotes: Alternatives checked: nectar fits the last clue but is the raw material, not the keeping food of clues one and four; beeswax and honeycomb are the store rather than what is stored; syrup and treacle are not made by bees and do not match the six-sided cells.
